tone_statements.quote: In their phonologies, members of the West-Central Family are characterised by the presence of palatalised consonant phonemes and the universal appearance of complex tonal systems. The glottal stop phoneme is absent, and so are complex syllable structures.

sources.citation: Franklin, Karl J. 2023. Samberigi (Sau) and Kewa. Language & Linguistics in Melanesia 41: 51-65.
sources.note: Sec. 'SAMBERIGI PHONOLOGY' (pp. 52-53) is a consonant chart (p t k h; prenasalized b d g; m n l r s w y) and a vowel chart (i u e a ae o, all may be nasalized); the rest is a Sau:Kewa comparative wordlist, a -ke/-ki/-nki/-ko suffix rule and sound correspondences. No mention of stress, accent, tone or intonation anywhere in the 16 pages.

sources.citation: Franklin, Karl J. 1975. Comments on Proto-Engan. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 1, 263-275. Pacific Linguistics C-38.
sources.note: Comparative Engan phonology; Sau listed among Engan languages (p. 263). p. 267: 'There has been no discussion in this section of phonemic tone or vowel length.. Tone often disambiguates present day minimal pairs' (Kewa examples). No Sau stress statement.
sources.venue: New Guinea area languages and language study

sources.citation: Franklin, Karl J. 1973. Appendices. In Franklin (ed.), The linguistic situation in the Gulf District and adjacent areas, 539-592. Pacific Linguistics C-26.
sources.note: Appendix J.6 'Sau' (p. 591) is a 100-item wordlist with no stress marks and no phonological note; p. 184 legend 'SAU (West Central) Samberigi (Capell 1962); Okani or Tugi (AR 1921-22)'. Silent on stress.
sources.venue: The linguistic situation in the Gulf District and adjacent areas

sources.citation: MacDonald, George E. 1973. The Teberan language family. In K. J. Franklin (ed.), The linguistic situation in the Gulf District and adjacent areas, Papua New Guinea, 111-148. Pacific Linguistics C-26. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Sec. 3.51 'Phonological Features' p. 131 has short notes 'SAMBERIGI (Sau)' and 'TIRI (Sau)': consonants observed, vowels, t > [r] intervocalically, syllable patterns V CV CVV CVC, prenasalized-stop clusters. Nothing on stress or tone for Samberigi/Tiri (the adjacent Witu note explicitly says Witu 'features phonemic tone, length, stress', so the silence is not an omission of the topic in the chapter).
sources.venue: The linguistic situation in the Gulf District and adjacent areas, Papua New Guinea

sources.citation: Franklin, Karl J. 1968. Languages of the Gulf District: a preview. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 8, 18-44. Pacific Linguistics A-16.

sources.quote: In their phonologies, members of the West-Central Family are characterised by the presence of palatalised consonant phonemes and the universal appearance of complex tonal systems. The glottal stop phoneme is absent, and so are complex syllable structures.
sources.locator: p. 483, sec. 2.7.2.2.5.5 'The West-Central Family' (membership list with 'Sau (Samberigi)' on p. 470)
sources.note: Family-level typological statement only: the languages of the West-Central Family (Enga, Ipili, Huli, Angal/Mendi, Kewa dialects, Sau (Samberigi), with Wiru as family-level isolate) are characterised phonologically by palatalised consonants and 'the universal appearance of complex tonal systems'; no glottal stop, no complex syllables. No Sau-specific tone inventory, tone-bearing unit or examples are given anywhere in the chapter (a full-text search for stress/accent the full text: Sau appears only in the membership/population list).
sources.venue: New Guinea area languages and language study

sources.citation: Pugh-Kitingan, Jacqueline. 1982. Language communication and instrumental music in the Southern Highlands of Papua New Guinea - comments on the Huli and Samberigi cases. Musicology Australia (Musicology) 7(1): 104-119.
sources.tag: likely states tone; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: online with restricted access (login, paywall or limited view)
sources.note: The article treats 'language communication' (speech surrogacy) on musical instruments among the Huli - where the author elsewhere shows instrument melody follows Huli speech-tone - and the Samberigi; whether it states that Samberigi/Sau has lexical tone, or reports speech-tone imitation for Samberigi instruments, could not be checked. Worth opening: it is the only located publication pairing Samberigi with language/pitch communication.
